Where it began

Mitchell Starc was born on 30 January 1990 in Baulkham Hills, New South Wales. He started playing at nine for Northern Districts, and not as a bowler at all: he kept wicket. At Berala he sometimes kept and bowled in the same innings, which must have made for a busy afternoon.

After Homebush Boys High School came a rookie contract with New South Wales and a first-class debut in March 2009.

The player

His Test debut came on 1 December 2011 against New Zealand, with his baggy green handed over by Richie Benaud. The early years were stop and start, but by October 2026 he had played 109 Tests and taken 451 wickets at 26.19, with 19 five-wicket innings, four ten-wicket matches and a best of 7 for 58. That puts him tenth on the list of all Test wicket-takers.

In 2015 he was the leading wicket-taker in all international cricket, and late that year he bowled the fastest ball ever measured in a Test, at 160.4 km/h. In Sri Lanka in 2016 he took 24 wickets in three Tests, a record for a visiting fast bowler in a three-Test series in Asia, and reached his 100th Test wicket at Galle along the way. He was part of the side that won the 2023 World Test Championship final, and he is one of only five players to have won an ICC trophy in all three formats.

What made him special

Pace, swing and a full ball that arrived before the batter was quite ready for it. He had a knack for striking in the very first over, and he learned to make an old ball reverse as well as a new one swing.

In his early years the ball did not always land where he meant it to. Even then it could work out: in the 2013 Ashes one that strayed down the leg side still accounted for a well-set Alastair Cook. With the bat he has 2,516 Test runs and 13 fifties, and his highest score is 99, made in India in 2013. By October 2026 a Test hundred was the one item on his list still marked pending.

Away from the middle

He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, and in 2016 he became the first bowler in nine years to be named Australia's Test player of the year. In a Sheffield Shield match in 2017 he took a hat-trick in each innings, something nobody had managed before in that competition.

He also catches the ball in his own way, with his fingers pointing down where most Australians point them up. It is a habit from childhood, and it has served him well enough for 50 Test catches.

And finally

The boy who started out behind the stumps spent his career sending the ball through to the men standing there. Wicketkeepers around the world have him to thank for a good many catches, and a few sore palms.
